why: Comparing a transistor with a sink tap and a row of on-off cards helps your child explain how a tiny signal can control a much bigger flow.
teaser: Meet a tiny three-legged switch, see how a small signal opens a big flow, then flip paper cards to count in ones and zeros.
title: Transistors
question: How can something smaller than a fingernail control electricity?
idea: A transistor is a switch with no moving parts. A tiny signal on its middle leg opens or closes a path for a bigger flow of electricity. Made from silicon with a sprinkle of other atoms, billions of them flip on and off as ones and zeros inside every computer.

curiosity.intro: Start with a tiny black bead on three legs. Then follow it back to hot glass tubes, a sink tap, a pinch of sand, and a row of on-off cards.
curiosity.carryForward: Turn a tap a little, then ask what small push might be steering a bigger flow.

questions.question: What came before transistors?
questions.notice: Compare the tall glass tube with the tiny black bead beside it.
questions.say: Glass vacuum tubes. A tube was about as tall as a hand. It glowed, got hot and burned out like an old light bulb. One early computer needed about 18,000 tubes and filled a room. In 1947, three scientists built the first transistor from gold foil pressed onto a small crystal.
questions.try: Hold up your hand: an old tube was about that tall. Now look at your smallest fingernail. A transistor you can hold is smaller still. Find one thing in the room the size of each.

questions.question: How can a tiny push control a big flow?
questions.notice: Look at how little the tap handle has turned, and how big the stream is.
questions.say: A transistor has three legs. Electricity flows in one leg and out another, and the middle leg works like a tap handle. A tiny signal there opens the path for a much bigger flow. The name joins two words: transfer and resistor.
questions.try: At a sink, turn the tap handle just a little. Watch how a small turn lets a big stream through. Then turn it back and watch the stream stop.

questions.question: How can on-off switches count?
questions.notice: Count the light cards and the dark cards in the row.
questions.say: A transistor switch is on or off, and a computer treats on as one and off as zero. Each extra switch doubles the patterns. Eight switches can make 256 patterns, enough for every letter on a keyboard.
questions.try: Lay two paper scraps in a row: light side up is on, dark side up is off. How many different rows can you make? Add a third scrap and count again. Did the number double?

questions.question: How do billions fit on one chip?
questions.notice: Look through the lens at the tiny pattern on the chip.
questions.say: They are printed, not built one by one. Light shines through a stencil onto a silicon wafer, layer after layer. In many tiny transistors, the middle part never touches the path. It sits behind a thin wall and steers the flow with an unseen electric push.
questions.try: Cut a simple shape out of paper to make a stencil. Lay it on another sheet and rub a crayon across it. Print it three times. Chip makers print with light in a similar way.

beats.passage: Little Wonderer found a black bead about the size of a lentil, balanced on three thin silver legs, and wondered whether it was some kind of beetle. Leaning in with a magnifying glass, Big Wonderer explained that it was a transistor, one of the most common things people have ever made. This one is large enough to hold, yet most transistors are far too small to see. Billions of them switch on and off inside the machines around us, and almost nobody notices.
beats.prompt: Why can something so common go unnoticed?

beats.passage: Before transistors, machines controlled electricity with glass vacuum tubes, which were about as tall as a hand. Tubes glowed, grew hot, used a lot of power, and burned out like old light bulbs, so engineers spent hours replacing them. One early computer needed about 18,000 tubes and filled a whole room. In 1947, three scientists at a telephone laboratory built the first transistor from a sliver of gold foil pressed onto a small block of crystal. It was smaller, cooler, and much longer lasting.
beats.prompt: How did the transistor change what machines could be?

beats.passage: A transistor works a little like the tap on a sink, where a small turn of the handle lets a big stream of water rush through. Electricity flows in through one leg and out through another, and the middle leg acts like the handle. A tiny signal there opens or closes the path for a much bigger flow. That lets a transistor work as a switch, or as an amplifier that makes a weak signal stronger. The name joins two older words, transfer and resistor.
beats.prompt: What are the two jobs a transistor can do?

beats.passage: Most transistors are made of silicon, an element found in ordinary sand and rock. Pure silicon barely lets electricity through, so makers add a tiny sprinkle of other atoms, a step called doping, rather like a pinch of salt in a pot of soup. Some sprinkles leave extra electrons free to move, and others leave tiny gaps where electrons can hop. Layering the two kinds side by side creates a border that electricity can cross only when it is told to. That is why silicon is called a semiconductor.
beats.prompt: How does doping change what silicon can do?

beats.passage: Little Wonderer pointed along a row of eight paper cards, each turned light side up for on or dark side up for off, just like a row of transistor switches. Computers treat on as one and off as zero, and each one-or-zero is called a bit. With one card there are two patterns, with two cards there are four, and every extra card doubles the count. Eight cards can make 256 different patterns, enough for every letter, number and mark on a keyboard.
beats.prompt: How many patterns could nine cards make, and why?

beats.passage: A phone chip smaller than a fingernail can hold billions of transistors, so they cannot be built one at a time. Instead, light shines through a stencil called a mask to print their patterns onto a thin silicon wafer, layer after layer, a little like printing a picture many times over. In many modern transistors, the control part, called the gate, never touches the path at all. It sits behind a wall of glass-like material and steers the flow with an unseen electric push. Nothing moves, yet the path opens and closes.
beats.prompt: How can a gate control a path it never touches?

poem.title: A Gate With No Hinges
lines: Little Wonderer found a small bug on the floor,
with three skinny legs, and no head, and no more.
“It’s no bug,” said the big one. “It just looks that way.
It’s a transistor, flipping on, off, all the day.”
It hasn’t a lever. It won’t make a click.
It’s quiet as pudding, and quick, oh, so quick!
One teeny-small nudge on the leg in the middle
lets a big river through. (It’s a bit of a riddle.)
Big Wonderer said, “In one phone, I am told,
there are billions of these, far more than you’d hold.
They don’t count to ten, and they don’t count by twos.
They count ‘on’ and ‘off’ — that’s the only way they choose.”
So the little one whispered and gave it a pat:
“You’re a gate with no hinges. Imagine that!”
Then flipped every lamp in the house on and off,
saying “one,” saying “zero,” till the big one said, “Off!”
